Where an applicant possesses a criminal history or record of harm from outside the Society, additional restorative preparation shall be required prior to reapplication.

Such preparation shall be administered jointly by:

  • the Circle of Health & Healing, and
  • the Circle of Learning

Programs may include:

  • restorative therapy
  • ethical and civic education
  • conflict resolution training
  • psychological rehabilitation where appropriate

Applicants may be granted monitored Transient status to participate in these programs.

Depending on the nature of the offense, movement within the Society may be supervised or otherwise restricted during this period.

If reapplication is denied following completion of the program, three (3) civic cycles must pass before the applicant may again reapply and re-enter the restorative program.

Final determinations remain subject to the population stewardship framework administered by the Circle of Balance, ensuring that admissions never exceed the Society’s sustainable demographic capacity.

Through this appeals structure, the Society affirms its commitment to fairness, procedural integrity, and respect for individuals who seek to join its community.

Article XII — Amendments

The Immigration Codex may be amended through the legislative procedures established in the Constitution.

Amendments to this Codex must follow the same standards of transparency, deliberation, and civic oversight that govern all constitutional instruments within the Society.

Any proposed amendment shall be reviewed by the relevant civic Circles responsible for custodianship, governance, and population stewardship before being submitted to the legislative process.

The amendment process ensures that immigration policy can adapt to changing ecological conditions, demographic realities, and civic needs while remaining anchored to the constitutional principles of the Society.

No amendment to this Codex may conflict with the Constitution or undermine the Society’s foundational commitments to consent, ecological stewardship, and civic fairness.

Appendix I — Population Capacity Model

This appendix defines the framework used by the Society to determine its Maximum Sustainable Population (MSP). The MSP represents the highest population level the Society can responsibly support without degrading ecological systems, overburdening civic institutions, or reducing the quality of life for its citizens and residents.

The concept of Maximum Sustainable Population reflects the Society’s commitment to living within the natural and civic limits of its environment. Rather than pursuing growth for its own sake, the Society seeks to maintain a stable and balanced relationship between people, infrastructure, and the ecosystems that sustain life.

The Population Capacity Model ensures that immigration and population policy remain grounded in measurable realities rather than political pressure, ideological expansion, or short‑term economic incentives. By anchoring population policy to objective indicators, the Society preserves long‑term stability and protects the well‑being of both present and future generations.

The calculation of Maximum Sustainable Population shall consider the following core resource domains:

• food production capacity
• water availability
• housing infrastructure
• healthcare capacity
• energy production
• ecological carrying limits
• educational infrastructure

These domains represent the foundational systems required for a healthy and functioning society. Each system contributes to the overall capacity of the community to sustain its population without experiencing structural strain or ecological degradation.

Each domain shall be periodically assessed by the relevant civic Circles responsible for stewardship of those systems. For example, Circles responsible for agriculture, environmental stewardship, healthcare, infrastructure, and education shall contribute data relevant to their respective sectors.

Data from these assessments shall be integrated into the Population Capacity Model to determine the Society’s current sustainable population threshold. These assessments may include resource inventories, infrastructure utilization rates, ecological monitoring, and long‑term planning projections.

Population capacity shall always be determined by the lowest limiting resource. When any essential resource approaches its sustainable limit, that constraint establishes the maximum population the Society can responsibly support.

This principle, sometimes referred to as the limiting‑factor model, ensures that the Society does not mistakenly interpret abundance in one sector as justification for overall population growth when other systems remain constrained.

For example, a community may possess sufficient housing but lack adequate water availability, food production, or healthcare infrastructure. In such cases, population growth would place unsustainable pressure on those constrained systems.

By recognizing the most limited resource as the defining constraint, the Society protects itself from imbalances that could destabilize its ecological or civic systems.

Through this model, the Society maintains a balanced relationship between its population, its civic institutions, and the ecological systems upon which all life depends.

Periodic updates to this model shall be conducted through regular review cycles established by the relevant civic Circles. These reviews ensure that population planning remains responsive to changing environmental conditions, technological advancements, infrastructure improvements, and demographic shifts.

All updates to the Population Capacity Model shall be documented within the governance archives to maintain transparency and provide historical records that guide future planning, immigration policy, and infrastructure development.

Through responsible population stewardship, the Society affirms that long‑term stability and ecological balance must remain the foundation upon which its growth and prosperity are built.

Appendix II — Operational Population Buffer Model

This appendix defines the calculation and maintenance of the Operational Population Buffer (OPB). The OPB establishes a controlled margin between the Society’s current population and its Maximum Sustainable Population (MSP) as defined in Appendix I.

Operating at or near maximum capacity introduces risk to the stability of any complex system. Ecological fluctuations, infrastructure disruption, unexpected demographic changes, public health events, or external crises may place sudden demands on food systems, healthcare, housing, education, and energy production. When a society operates at the edge of its limits, even minor disruptions can cascade into systemic instability.

The Operational Population Buffer exists to prevent such fragility. By maintaining a deliberate margin between the current population and the maximum sustainable population, the Society preserves the flexibility required to absorb shocks without degrading essential services or ecological balance.

The purpose of the OPB is therefore preventative rather than restrictive. It represents a structural safeguard that allows the Society to operate within a stable and resilient operating range rather than at theoretical limits.

Through the use of a population buffer, the Society ensures that growth remains deliberate, sustainable, and responsive to real conditions rather than driven by short‑term pressures.

Section II.01 — Buffer Percentage Guidelines

The Operational Population Buffer shall be calculated as a percentage margin below the Maximum Sustainable Population.

This percentage establishes the difference between:

• Maximum Sustainable Population (MSP)
• Current Population (CP)

The buffer percentage represents the minimum reserve capacity the Society maintains at all times. This reserve allows civic systems to function comfortably within their limits rather than constantly approaching them.

The buffer percentage shall be periodically reviewed by the relevant civic Circles responsible for infrastructure, ecological stewardship, and population planning. These reviews allow the Society to adjust the buffer in response to technological advances, infrastructure improvements, ecological change, or demographic trends.

The selected buffer must be sufficient to account for normal demographic variation, seasonal resource fluctuations, infrastructure maintenance cycles, and temporary strain on civic institutions.

Maintaining an adequate buffer ensures that growth remains gradual and controlled rather than reactive.

Section II.02 — Birth Reserve Methodology

The Operational Population Buffer must also account for natural population growth within the Society. Births represent a predictable yet variable source of population increase that must be integrated into long‑term planning.

A portion of the Operational Population Buffer shall therefore be reserved as a Birth Reserve. This reserve ensures that natural demographic growth can occur without immediately forcing population levels to approach or exceed the Maximum Sustainable Population.

Birth reserve calculations shall be informed by historical birth rates, projected demographic trends, generational planning models, and expected long‑term population distribution across age groups.

This approach allows the Society to welcome new generations without immediately restricting immigration or placing strain on civic infrastructure.

By reserving capacity for births, the Society recognizes that population stability must include the natural rhythms of family formation and generational continuity.

Section II.03 — Emergency Reserve Thresholds

In addition to demographic planning, the Operational Population Buffer shall include an Emergency Reserve Threshold.

This reserve protects the Society’s ability to respond to unexpected circumstances such as ecological disruption, infrastructure damage, public health emergencies, natural disasters, or humanitarian intake scenarios.

Maintaining an emergency reserve allows the Society to temporarily accommodate population pressures without destabilizing critical systems or forcing immediate population restrictions.

Emergency reserves may be activated, expanded, or adjusted through review by the appropriate civic Circles when extraordinary conditions arise.

The presence of this reserve ensures that the Society retains flexibility in times of crisis while still maintaining long‑term population stability.

Section II.04 — Monitoring and Adjustment

The Operational Population Buffer shall be monitored through regular population reviews conducted by the civic Circles responsible for demographic planning, infrastructure management, and ecological stewardship.

Population data, demographic projections, and infrastructure capacity metrics shall be reviewed at defined intervals to ensure that the buffer remains sufficient to protect civic stability.

If population levels approach the buffer threshold, immigration intake may be temporarily reduced, slowed, or paused until sufficient capacity has been restored.

Such adjustments are not punitive but represent responsible stewardship of the Society’s population system.

Adjustments to the OPB must remain consistent with the broader Population Capacity Model defined in Appendix I.

Through continuous monitoring and adaptive management, the Society maintains a population system that is resilient, transparent, and responsive to changing conditions.

Appendix III — Immigration Capacity Formula

This appendix defines the mathematical framework used to determine Available Immigration Capacity (AIC) for each immigration cycle.

The AIC represents the number of new residents that may safely enter the Hopeful evaluation and residency pathways without exceeding the limits established by the Population Capacity Model and Operational Population Buffer.

By formalizing this calculation, the Society ensures that immigration decisions remain consistent, transparent, and grounded in measurable conditions rather than political pressure, administrative discretion, or short‑term demands.

The Immigration Capacity Formula transforms population stewardship from a subjective judgment into a clearly defined planning tool.

Section III.01 — Core Formula Structure

The Available Immigration Capacity for any given cycle shall be determined using the following formula:

AIC = MSP − (CP + OPB + PNG)

Where:

• AIC = Available Immigration Capacity
• MSP = Maximum Sustainable Population
• CP = Current Population
• OPB = Operational Population Buffer
• PNG = Projected Natural Population Growth

This equation ensures that immigration intake remains safely within the limits of sustainable population management.

By accounting for both existing population levels and expected demographic growth, the formula prevents immigration intake from pushing the Society beyond its safe operating range.

Section III.02 — Variable Descriptions

Each variable within the formula represents a measurable component of the Society’s population system.

Maximum Sustainable Population (MSP) represents the ecological and infrastructural limit determined through the Population Capacity Model defined in Appendix I.

Current Population (CP) represents the total number of citizens, residents, and recognized Independents currently residing within the Society.

Operational Population Buffer (OPB) represents the safety margin maintained below MSP to ensure resilience, adaptability, and systemic stability.

Projected Natural Population Growth (PNG) represents anticipated population increases resulting from births or other internal demographic changes during the upcoming immigration cycle.

Together these variables ensure that immigration intake remains aligned with real population conditions rather than theoretical capacity.

Section III.03 — Transient Load Adjustments

Transient residents contribute to infrastructure demand during their period of residence. For the purposes of population calculations, each Transient shall count toward the Current Population (CP) for the duration of their authorized stay.

If a Transient transitions to citizenship, they remain included in population calculations without interruption.

Transient Load Adjustments may also be applied for short‑term research initiatives, infrastructure projects, or temporary civic deployments when approved by the appropriate Circles.

All transient adjustments must remain temporary and shall not be used to justify sustained population expansion beyond sustainable limits.

Section III.04 — Infrastructure Expansion Adjustment

When new housing, energy production systems, food production infrastructure, healthcare capacity, educational institutions, or other major civic resources are expanded, the Maximum Sustainable Population may increase accordingly.

Infrastructure expansion adjustments must be verified through assessment by the relevant civic Circles responsible for those systems.

These assessments ensure that projected infrastructure capacity reflects operational reality rather than theoretical or incomplete development.

Section III.05 — Worked Examples

The following examples illustrate how the Immigration Capacity Formula is applied.

Example 1 — Stable Growth Scenario

MSP = 100,000
CP = 82,000
OPB = 10,000
PNG = 4,000

AIC = 100,000 − (82,000 + 10,000 + 4,000)

AIC = 4,000

Under these conditions, 4,000 additional individuals may be admitted during the upcoming immigration cycle without exceeding sustainable limits.

Example 2 — Near Capacity Scenario

MSP = 100,000
CP = 90,000
OPB = 8,000
PNG = 3,000

AIC = 100,000 − (90,000 + 8,000 + 3,000)

AIC = -1,000

Because the result is negative, the Society is already operating within the buffer range and no immigration admissions would occur during that cycle.

This example demonstrates how the formula automatically prevents population growth when the Society approaches its safe operating limits.

Section III.06 — Transparency Principle

The Immigration Capacity Formula exists to ensure that immigration policy remains governed by ecological and infrastructural reality rather than political pressure.

All calculations used to determine Available Immigration Capacity shall remain transparent, publicly auditable, and documented within the Society’s governance records.

By maintaining visibility of these calculations, the Society reinforces public trust and ensures that population stewardship remains consistent, fair, and grounded in measurable conditions.

Through the use of this model, immigration policy remains aligned with long‑term sustainability rather than short‑term administrative discretion.

Daughter Document of the Circle of Balance
Article I — Purpose of the Codex
The Immigration Codex establishes the principles and procedures governing entry into the Society, evaluation of immigration applicants, residency classifications, pathways to citizenship, population stewardship, and departure or repatriation.
Its purpose is to ensure that immigration strengthens the Society while preserving ecological balance, civic harmony, and constitutional integrity.
The Codex does not determine who may aspire to membership. Rather, it governs how applications for membership are evaluated, ensuring that admission decisions remain transparent, principled, and aligned with the long‑term stability of the Society.
Immigration is recognized as both an opportunity and a responsibility. Individuals who seek entry bring knowledge, culture, and skill that may enrich the community, while the Society retains the duty to safeguard its ecological limits, civic institutions, and social cohesion.
Accordingly, the procedures defined in this Codex are designed to balance openness with stewardship. Admission is neither automatic nor arbitrary. It is conducted through structured evaluation, guided by the Constitution and administered through the appropriate civic Circles.
Through this framework, immigration remains compatible with the Society’s founding commitments to consent, contribution, ecological stewardship, and the preservation of a stable and flourishing civilization.
Article II — Constitutional Foundation of Membership
Immigration governance derives its authority from Article II of the Constitution: Membership & Citizenship. The principles articulated within the Constitution establish the philosophical and legal framework through which membership in the Society is understood.
Accordingly, the following foundations guide all immigration policy and evaluation procedures:
Voluntary Membership — Membership in the Society is voluntary. No individual is compelled to join, remain within, or adopt the civic covenant of the community.
Right to Seek Entry — No person approaching the Society in good faith shall be barred from seeking entry. The Society recognizes that aspiration toward membership is itself an expression of goodwill and curiosity.
Equality of Consideration — Admission decisions shall never be determined by bloodline, ancestry, wealth, nationality, religion, or coercive influence. Membership is not an inherited privilege nor a purchased entitlement.
Covenant of Intent — Citizenship is a covenant entered through conscious commitment to the Society’s principles. It is defined by intent, participation, and contribution rather than lineage.
Sacred Right of Exit — The right of peaceful exit from the Society remains sacred and inviolable. No individual shall be prevented from departing should they choose to relinquish membership.
Within this constitutional framework, the Immigration Codex governs the procedures by which membership applications are evaluated. The Codex does not determine who may aspire to membership, but establishes the structured process through which that aspiration is examined in alignment with the long-term stability and ethical foundations of the Society.
Article III — Population Stewardship
The Society maintains its population within carefully managed and sustainable limits in order to preserve ecological balance, civic stability, and a high quality of life for all members of the community. Population stewardship is therefore recognized as a central responsibility of the Circle of Custodianship and as an essential safeguard for the long‑term flourishing and resilience of the Society.
Responsibility for monitoring ecological capacity, demographic balance, and long-term population sustainability rests with the Circle of Balance, which maintains the Society’s demographic thresholds and environmental carrying-capacity assessments.
Population levels influence every aspect of communal life: the availability of resources, the health of ecosystems, the reliability of infrastructure, and the stability of civic institutions. Responsible population stewardship ensures that growth never occurs at the expense of environmental integrity or the well‑being of existing citizens. By maintaining population within sustainable boundaries, the Society protects not only present prosperity but also the inheritance of future generations.
Unlike many historical societies that expanded without regard for environmental limits or long‑term sustainability, the Society recognizes that every territory possesses finite resources and ecological thresholds. Population policy must therefore reflect the carrying capacity of the land, the resilience of ecological systems, and the infrastructure required to support a thriving and balanced community.
The purpose of population stewardship is not to restrict opportunity but to ensure that opportunity remains available to all who live within the Society. A population that grows beyond the capacity of its environment inevitably produces scarcity, instability, and inequality. By contrast, a population maintained within sustainable limits allows resources to remain abundant, ecosystems to remain healthy, and civic harmony to endure.
Section 3.01 — Maximum Sustainable Population
Custodianship shall establish and maintain the Maximum Sustainable Population (MSP) of the Society. This value represents the highest population level that can be supported without degrading ecological health, exhausting critical resources, or undermining civic stability.
The MSP serves as a structural boundary within which the Society can prosper. It ensures that the needs of the population remain aligned with the capacity of the environment and the strength of the Society’s infrastructure.
The determination of MSP shall consider, at minimum:
• food production capacity
• freshwater availability
• housing and infrastructure capacity
• healthcare system capability
• energy production
• ecological impact and regeneration limits
Additional considerations may include the resilience of local ecosystems, the availability of essential materials, transportation infrastructure, and the capacity of civic institutions to support community well‑being.
The methodology used to calculate the Maximum Sustainable Population shall be defined in Appendix I — Population Capacity Model. This model provides the analytical framework through which Custodianship evaluates environmental capacity, infrastructure readiness, and long‑term sustainability.
Section 3.02 — Operational Population Buffer
The Society shall intentionally maintain its active population below the Maximum Sustainable Population through the use of an Operational Population Buffer (OPB).
The Operational Population Buffer ensures that the Society does not operate at the edge of its ecological or infrastructural limits. By maintaining a margin below maximum capacity, the Society preserves flexibility and resilience in the face of change.
This buffer preserves adaptive space within the population system and allows the Society to respond to demographic changes without destabilizing civic or ecological systems. The buffer provides capacity for:
• births within the citizen population
• approved immigration admissions
• unforeseen demographic fluctuations
• infrastructure disruptions or environmental stress
Maintaining a population buffer also protects the Society from sudden strain caused by environmental events, resource variability, or infrastructure maintenance cycles. By preserving available capacity, the Society can adapt without resorting to emergency restrictions or destabilizing policy changes.
The calculation and maintenance of the Operational Population Buffer shall be defined in Appendix II — Operational Population Buffer Model, which describes the technical methodology used to determine appropriate buffer levels.
Section 3.03 — Population Monitoring
Custodianship shall maintain continuous monitoring of demographic movement within the Society. Accurate and transparent population data is essential to responsible stewardship and effective immigration policy.
Population monitoring shall include the tracking of:
• births
• deaths
• immigration admissions
• voluntary departures
• Independent status transitions
Additional demographic data may also be maintained to support long‑term planning, including trends in household formation, generational change, and infrastructure usage.
This information allows Custodianship to maintain a real‑time understanding of population dynamics and ensures that immigration decisions remain consistent with ecological limits and infrastructure capacity. The data gathered through population monitoring shall inform the population capacity calculations described in the appendices and guide responsible immigration policy.
Section 3.04 — Population Review Cycle
Custodianship shall periodically review the Maximum Sustainable Population to ensure that the population framework remains aligned with current ecological conditions, technological development, and infrastructure capacity.
Over time, improvements in sustainability practices, agricultural efficiency, renewable energy production, water management, and infrastructure design may expand the Society’s ability to responsibly support additional population. Conversely, environmental degradation or resource limitations may require the Society to adjust its population expectations.
Adjustments to the MSP may therefore occur when improvements in sustainability, resource management, or infrastructure expand the Society’s ability to support additional population without compromising environmental integrity or civic stability.
All revisions to MSP calculations shall remain consistent with the methodologies defined in the Population Capacity Model. Any adjustments to the MSP shall be conducted transparently and supported by clear ecological and infrastructural evidence to ensure continued trust in the stewardship process.
Article IV — Residency Classifications
Membership within the Society is expressed through clearly defined civic classifications. These classifications provide structure for the immigration process and ensure that individuals interacting with the Society are recognized according to their relationship with its civic covenant and institutions.
Residency classifications clarify rights, responsibilities, expectations, and limitations while maintaining transparency in population accounting and immigration governance. Each classification reflects a distinct stage of relationship with the Society’s constitutional framework, its cultural norms, and its civic responsibilities.
By establishing these classifications, the Society ensures that individuals interacting with its territory and institutions are clearly recognized according to their civic standing. This clarity protects the integrity of the immigration system, supports accurate population stewardship, and preserves the distinction between visitors, prospective members, residents, and full citizens.
The classifications defined within this Article allow the Society to welcome visitors, evaluate prospective members, and recognize full citizens while preserving clear legal boundaries between these statuses. These distinctions ensure that civic rights and responsibilities remain proportional to the level of commitment an individual has made to the Society.
Each classification represents a different relationship to the Society’s covenant. Some represent aspiration toward membership, others represent participation within the community, and others exist to manage temporary presence or voluntary departure from civic life.
Section 4.01 — Citizen
A Citizen is a full covenant member of the Society. Citizenship represents a conscious and voluntary commitment to the constitutional principles, civic responsibilities, and cultural norms that sustain the community.
Citizens possess full civic standing within the Society. This includes participation in civic processes, access to communal resources, and the responsibility to contribute to the ongoing well-being, stability, and development of the community.
Citizens participate in the governance structures of the Society through the appropriate Circles and civic institutions. They are recognized as stewards of the Society’s constitutional values and share responsibility for protecting its ecological balance, social harmony, and institutional integrity.
Citizenship is not inherited automatically by lineage alone, nor purchased through wealth or influence. Rather, it is entered through demonstrated commitment to the principles of consent, contribution, ecological stewardship, and civic harmony. Citizenship therefore represents both a privilege and a responsibility shared among those who choose to participate in the Society’s covenant.
Section 4.02 — Resident
A Resident is an individual who has been admitted into the Society through the immigration process but has not yet entered the full covenant of citizenship.
Residents live and contribute within the Society while undergoing a period of civic integration. During this phase, individuals participate in the social, cultural, educational, and economic systems of the community while demonstrating their compatibility with its institutions and values.
Residency serves as a period of mutual observation and adaptation. The Society evaluates the individual’s contribution, conduct, and cultural integration, while the individual gains firsthand experience of life within the Society before choosing whether to enter the full covenant of citizenship.
This stage allows individuals to become familiar with the Society’s civic expectations, cultural practices, and community structures. It also allows the Society to confirm that long-term membership will strengthen the community rather than destabilize it.
Section 4.03 — Hopeful
A Hopeful is an individual who has formally declared their intention to seek membership within the Society and has entered the immigration evaluation process.
Hopeful status reflects aspiration rather than membership. Individuals in this classification are recognized as applicants who wish to join the Society but have not yet been admitted into residency.
Hopefuls remain outside the Society’s official population count until they are admitted into residency. This distinction ensures that population stewardship calculations remain accurate while allowing the Society to fairly evaluate individuals who wish to join the community.
The Hopeful classification ensures that individuals seeking entry are treated with dignity, transparency, and procedural fairness while allowing the Society to evaluate compatibility with its civic covenant.
Section 4.04 — Transient
A Transient is an individual temporarily residing within the Society for a clearly defined and limited purpose. Transient presence does not constitute immigration or residency and does not imply future citizenship.
The transient classification allows the Society to benefit from academic exchange, collaborative knowledge sharing, and specialized expertise while preserving the integrity of its immigration and population systems.
Transient entry may occur only through two recognized avenues:
Section 4.04(a) — Academic Exchange
Administered by the Circle of Learning, this avenue includes:
• foreign exchange students
• visiting professors
• research scholars
• educational collaborators
These individuals participate in the Society’s academic and intellectual life while contributing to the exchange of knowledge between institutions. Academic exchange strengthens the intellectual vitality of the Society while allowing learning institutions to maintain relationships with the wider world.
Section 4.04(b) — Sector Contribution
Administered by the Circle of Balance, this avenue allows the Society to temporarily receive specialized expertise or labor not yet available through its own educational systems. Information is gathered from the Circle of Contribution regarding civic and sector demand, from the Circle of Learning regarding educational supply and training capacity, and from the Circle of Balance regarding population sustainability and demographic thresholds.
This mechanism allows the Society to develop new infrastructure, train future specialists, or temporarily address gaps within critical sectors while its educational institutions prepare future graduates.
Examples may include:
• specialized technical expertise
• infrastructure development
• sector mentorship
• training of future graduates
Section 4.04(c) — Duration of Presence
Transient residency shall not exceed five years. Transient status may not be renewed beyond this term.
This limitation ensures that transient presence remains temporary and does not function as an indirect pathway to permanent residency outside of the established immigration framework.
Individuals wishing to remain beyond this period must apply through the Hopeful evaluation process and enter the standard immigration pathway.
Section 4.04(d) — Good Standing
Transients must respect the Constitution and Charters of the Society and conduct themselves in accordance with the principles of consent, stewardship, and civic harmony.
While residing within the Society, Transients are expected to respect its cultural norms, ecological practices, and civic expectations.
Violation of these expectations may result in the revocation of transient status and termination of their presence within the Society.
Section 4.04(e) — Priority Pathway
A Transient who completes their term in good standing and demonstrates meaningful contribution to the Society may receive elevated priority when applying through the Hopeful process.
This priority reflects demonstrated participation in the life of the community and recognizes individuals who have already contributed positively to the Society.
However, priority consideration does not guarantee admission into residency or citizenship. All applicants must still complete the standard evaluation process.
Section 4.05 — Independent
An Independent is a former citizen who has relinquished civic membership under the procedures defined in the Restoration Codex.
Independents no longer participate in the civic covenant of the Society and are no longer considered members of its civic body. However, the Society recognizes the sacred right of peaceful exit and therefore provides a structured transition period for individuals who choose to withdraw from citizenship.
During this transition period, Independents may remain temporarily within the Society’s territory while preparing for departure in accordance with the Restoration Codex.
Independent status exists to preserve the sacred right of peaceful exit while ensuring that the Society maintains clear civic boundaries between active citizens and those who have voluntarily withdrawn from membership.
Article V — Immigration Admission System
The Society regulates immigration through a structured admission system designed to maintain ecological balance, civic stability, and fairness in the evaluation of applicants. Immigration decisions must remain consistent with the population stewardship principles established in Article III and the constitutional foundations defined in Article II.
The admission system ensures that entry into the Society occurs through transparent procedures rather than arbitrary discretion. Every applicant is evaluated through a defined process that considers civic compatibility, contribution potential, and the available population capacity of the Society.
Immigration is therefore neither unrestricted nor exclusionary. Instead, it operates within a framework that balances openness with responsibility, allowing the Society to welcome new members while preserving the sustainability of its institutions, its ecological limits, and the long‑term stability of the community.
The purpose of this admission system is not merely to regulate entry, but to ensure that immigration strengthens the Society. New residents are expected to contribute meaningfully to civic life, respect the constitutional principles of the community, and participate constructively in its cultural and ecological stewardship.
By maintaining a structured immigration system, the Society protects itself from the instability that can arise when population growth exceeds infrastructure, environmental capacity, or civic integration. At the same time, the system ensures that individuals who genuinely seek to participate in the Society’s covenant are given a fair and transparent path toward membership.
Section 5.01 — Immigration Capacity
Admissions into residency are limited by the available population capacity of the Society. Immigration decisions must remain consistent with the Maximum Sustainable Population (MSP) and the Operational Population Buffer (OPB) defined in Article III.
Population stewardship requires that immigration decisions reflect the ecological and infrastructural realities of the Society. Growth that exceeds sustainable capacity would place strain on resources, degrade environmental systems, and undermine the stability of civic institutions. For this reason, immigration capacity must always remain subordinate to the long‑term sustainability of the community.
The number of applicants who may be admitted during any evaluation cycle shall therefore be determined by the Immigration Capacity Formula defined in Appendix III — Immigration Capacity Formula.
This formula evaluates available population space by considering multiple factors including:
• current population levels
• the Maximum Sustainable Population
• the Operational Population Buffer
• demographic changes including births and deaths
• infrastructure capacity and resource availability
Additional inputs may include infrastructure expansion, improvements in sustainability practices, or changes in environmental conditions that affect the Society’s ability to responsibly support additional population.
Only when sufficient capacity exists may additional residents be admitted through the immigration process. When capacity is limited, the Society must prioritize stability over expansion.
Section 5.02 — Population Priority
When available immigration capacity is limited, admission decisions shall follow a defined order of priority designed to preserve fairness while recognizing demonstrated commitment to the Society.
Priority shall be granted in the following order:
Citizens and their children
Transients applying for residency through the Hopeful process who have completed their term in good standing
External Hopeful applicants
This structure recognizes that individuals who have already participated in the life of the Society may be better understood by the community than applicants whose compatibility has not yet been directly observed.
Transients who have contributed through academic exchange or sector service possess a demonstrated history within the Society’s institutions and cultural environment. Granting them priority consideration reflects the value of proven contribution while still maintaining the integrity of the evaluation process.
At the same time, the Society remains open to external applicants who wish to join the community and contribute to its development. The priority system does not exclude new applicants but ensures that admissions occur in a manner consistent with population stewardship and civic stability.
Section 5.03 — Immigration Pause
When the population approaches the Maximum Sustainable Population or when the Operational Population Buffer cannot be maintained, the Society shall temporarily pause the admission of new residents.
An immigration pause protects ecological systems, infrastructure capacity, and the stability of the community. Operating continuously at the maximum population threshold would remove the adaptive flexibility required to respond to demographic changes, environmental stress, or infrastructure maintenance.
During periods in which an immigration pause is active, Hopeful applications may continue to be submitted, evaluated, and recorded. However, admissions into residency shall not occur until population capacity becomes available.
Maintaining this separation between evaluation and admission allows the Society to preserve fairness within the immigration process while still honoring the ecological limits defined by population stewardship.
Once capacity is restored through demographic change, infrastructure expansion, or ecological improvement, immigration admissions may resume according to the procedures defined in this Codex.
Section 5.04 — Transparency of Admissions
Immigration decisions shall be conducted with transparency, procedural integrity, and accountability to the constitutional principles of the Society.
The Circles responsible for evaluation shall document admission decisions and maintain records that demonstrate adherence to the procedures defined in this Codex. These records ensure that decisions can be reviewed and that the immigration system remains free from favoritism, corruption, or arbitrary decision‑making.
Transparency also protects applicants by ensuring that the evaluation process remains consistent and fair. By maintaining clear documentation of decisions and procedures, the Society reinforces public trust in its immigration governance and ensures that admission policies remain aligned with the values of consent, contribution, and stewardship that define the civic covenant.
Article VI — Hopeful Evaluation Process
The Hopeful Evaluation Process establishes the procedures through which individuals seeking membership in the Society are assessed for compatibility with its constitutional principles, civic expectations, and ecological responsibilities.
The purpose of this evaluation is not to judge personal worth, cultural origin, nationality, or personal history. Rather, the process exists to determine whether an applicant can live constructively within the Society’s covenant of consent, contribution, stewardship, and civic harmony. The evaluation recognizes that individuals come from diverse backgrounds and social systems, and therefore focuses primarily on present intentions, character, and the applicant’s willingness to adapt to the Society’s civic framework.
All applicants entering the immigration process shall be recognized under the classification of Hopeful. During this stage, the Society evaluates the applicant’s intentions, character, and potential contribution while the applicant gains a clearer understanding of the Society’s expectations, responsibilities, and cultural norms.
The Hopeful period is therefore a reciprocal process of discovery. While the Society evaluates the applicant’s compatibility with its principles, the applicant is equally encouraged to determine whether the Society’s civic philosophy, naturalist traditions, and communal expectations align with their own values and aspirations.
The evaluation process is designed to be transparent, respectful, and free from arbitrary decision-making. It is administered collectively through the civic Circles to ensure that no single authority determines the outcome of an application. Decisions regarding admission must reflect the considered judgment of multiple civic institutions acting in cooperation.
This structure protects both the Society and the applicant from bias, favoritism, or unilateral control over the immigration process.
Section 6.01 — Declaration of Intent
Applicants seeking entry into the Society must formally declare their intention to pursue membership. This declaration affirms that the applicant understands the Society’s constitutional principles and wishes to be considered for residency within its civic framework.
The declaration also confirms that the applicant approaches the Society in good faith and is willing to participate in the evaluation process with honesty, transparency, and respect for its procedures.
Applicants are encouraged to provide a brief personal statement explaining their motivations for seeking membership, their understanding of the Society’s principles, and the ways in which they believe they may contribute to the community if admitted.
This declaration does not function as a test of ideology. Its purpose is simply to establish clarity of intention and to ensure that applicants approach the process with sincerity and openness.
Section 6.02 — Good-Faith Review
The Circles responsible for immigration evaluation shall conduct a preliminary review to determine whether the applicant has approached the Society in good faith.
This review considers the sincerity of the applicant’s intentions, their willingness to engage constructively with the process, and the absence of coercive, deceptive, or exploitative motives.
The review may include examination of prior conduct, professional history, and available references where appropriate, though the Society recognizes that individuals may seek new beginnings and therefore does not judge applicants solely by their past circumstances.
Applicants who demonstrate clear bad faith, deliberate deception, intent to exploit the Society’s systems, or an explicit intention to undermine the Society’s constitutional principles may be denied further consideration.
Such denials must be documented and justified within the immigration record to ensure accountability within the evaluation process.
Section 6.03 — Civic Compatibility Review
Applicants shall be evaluated for compatibility with the Society’s core civic values, including:
• consent
• contribution
• ecological stewardship
• lifelong learning
• restorative accountability
This review focuses on the applicant’s understanding of these principles and their willingness to participate in a society structured around them.
Compatibility assessment does not require ideological uniformity. Diversity of perspective, philosophy, and personal belief is welcome within the Society, provided that applicants respect the constitutional framework and civic covenant that sustain the community.
Applicants are therefore evaluated not for agreement with every aspect of the Society’s philosophy, but for their willingness to coexist peacefully within a system that prioritizes consent, mutual responsibility, and ecological care.
Section 6.04 — Contribution Alignment
The Circle of Contribution, Circle of Learning, and Circle of Balance shall jointly evaluate the applicant’s knowledge, skills, experience, and the Society’s current population capacity.
This evaluation recognizes that every individual possesses abilities that may benefit the community in different ways. Contributions may include professional expertise, skilled labor, educational knowledge, artistic work, caregiving, research, technical development, or other forms of meaningful participation within the Society’s sectors.
Where an applicant’s primary expertise corresponds to an existing sector need, the individual may be considered for direct integration within that sector. Where existing roles are already fulfilled, alternative avenues of contribution may be identified.
Applicants are not required to enter the Society with a predefined occupational role. However, admission into residency requires a demonstrated willingness to contribute to the Society in meaningful ways, including participation in sectors that support the community’s stability, sustainability, and long-term development.
Section 6.05 — Capacity Review
Applicants may only be admitted into residency when population capacity allows as determined by the Circle of Balance.
The availability of residency positions shall be determined according to the immigration capacity calculations defined in Appendix III. These calculations account for housing availability, ecological sustainability, civic infrastructure, and sector workforce needs.
Even applicants who successfully complete all stages of evaluation may be deferred if population capacity does not permit admission at the time of evaluation.
Deferral does not constitute rejection. Applicants may remain eligible for future admission when capacity permits, provided they maintain good standing within the evaluation process.
This safeguard ensures that immigration remains aligned with the Society’s commitment to ecological balance and responsible population management.
Section 6.06 — Multi-Circle Interview Panels
All formal applicant interviews shall be conducted by a panel drawn from multiple civic Circles.
This multi-circle structure ensures that immigration decisions incorporate diverse perspectives from the Society’s institutions and prevents any single authority from determining the outcome of an application.
Interview panels may include representatives from relevant sectors such as Learning, Contribution, Health & Healing, Harmony, or other Circles whose perspectives may assist in evaluating the applicant’s compatibility with the Society.
Panel members are responsible for conducting interviews with professionalism, respect, and impartiality. The purpose of these interviews is not interrogation but dialogue, allowing both the applicant and the Society to better understand one another.
Section 6.07 — Transparency of Proceedings
All evaluation interviews shall be recorded and archived as part of the Society’s governance records.
This documentation protects both applicants and the Society by ensuring that the evaluation process remains transparent, accountable, and open to review if questions arise regarding procedural fairness.
Recorded proceedings may be reviewed by relevant civic oversight bodies if disputes arise concerning the conduct or outcome of an evaluation.
The maintenance of transparent records ensures that the immigration process remains consistent with the Society’s broader commitment to accountable governance.
Section 6.08 — Cultural Norm Transparency
Applicants shall be informed in advance of the cultural norms practiced within the Society, including its naturalist traditions and attitudes toward the human body.
Because the Society maintains a cultural environment that differs from many external societies, it is essential that applicants understand these norms prior to entering the evaluation environment.
Interview environments may reflect these norms, including states of dress or undress common within the community. Applicants may choose their state of dress or undress during the evaluation process, nor will their comfort level in the moment be treated as a determining factor in their evaluation.
Compatibility assessment shall focus on the applicant’s understanding of these cultural norms and their willingness to respect them within the Society, rather than momentary emotional responses during the interview.
Section 6.09 — Evaluation Outcomes
At the conclusion of the evaluation process, applications may result in one of the following outcomes:
• acceptance into residency
• deferred admission pending population capacity or further review
• denial due to incompatibility with the Society’s constitutional framework
All decisions shall be documented and communicated clearly to the applicant.
Where an application is denied, the decision must include a brief explanation outlining the reasoning behind the determination. This ensures that the process remains transparent and respectful even when admission cannot be granted.
The goal of the Hopeful Evaluation Process is not exclusion, but careful integration. By ensuring that each new member enters the Society with clarity of intention and understanding of its civic responsibilities, the process protects the long-term stability and harmony of the community.
Article VII — Residency Pathway
The Residency Pathway establishes the process through which a Hopeful transitions from applicant status into full citizenship within the Society. This pathway is designed to allow both the individual and the community sufficient time to determine whether long‑term integration is appropriate and sustainable.
Residency serves as a period of lived participation within the Society’s civic framework. During this time the resident learns the daily practices, responsibilities, and cultural rhythms of the community while contributing to its stability and development.
The Residency Pathway exists to ensure that citizenship is not granted through ideology alone, but through demonstrated participation, trust, and mutual compatibility.
Section 7.01 — Provisional Residency
Applicants who successfully complete the Hopeful Evaluation Process may be granted Provisional Residency.
Provisional residents are permitted to live and work within the Society while participating in its civic institutions and cultural life. During this period they begin contributing to the community through the sectors aligned with their skills and interests.
Provisional residency allows both the individual and the Society to evaluate long‑term compatibility under real conditions of community life.
Section 7.02 — Rights of Residents
Residents shall be afforded the fundamental protections of the Society during their period of residency.
These protections include access to housing, healthcare, education, and participation in communal life consistent with the Society’s constitutional framework.
Residents may participate in civic discussions and community activities but shall not exercise voting authority within constitutional governance until full citizenship is granted.
This structure preserves the integrity of the Society’s decision‑making processes while still integrating residents meaningfully into community life.
Section 7.03 — Contribution Participation
Residents are expected to participate in the Society’s systems of contribution in a manner consistent with their abilities, knowledge, and physical capacity.
Contribution may occur through professional sectors, skilled labor, research, education, caregiving, artistic production, ecological stewardship, or other forms of meaningful work that support the community while remaining consistent with population capacity determined by the Circle of Balance.
The purpose of contribution during residency is not merely productivity, but the cultivation of mutual trust between the resident and the community.
Through participation, residents demonstrate their willingness to support the Society’s stability and shared responsibilities.
Section 7.04 — Cultural Integration
Residents are encouraged to engage with the Society’s cultural practices, traditions, and naturalist values during the residency period.
Integration includes learning the Society’s civic customs, participating in community gatherings, and developing familiarity with its principles of consent, stewardship, and communal responsibility.
Cultural integration does not require abandonment of personal identity, heritage, or belief. The Society values diversity of background and perspective so long as residents respect the constitutional covenant that sustains the community.
Section 7.05 — Residency Review
At defined intervals during the residency period, civic Circles may review the resident’s integration into the community.
These reviews focus on the resident’s participation, contribution, conduct within the community, and continued compatibility with the Society’s civic framework.
Reviews are intended to be constructive and supportive rather than punitive. Their purpose is to identify any challenges in integration and provide guidance that assists the resident in successfully adapting to community life.
Section 7.06 — Eligibility for Citizenship
Residents who demonstrate sustained compatibility with the Society’s principles and who actively contribute to community life may become eligible for citizenship.
Eligibility shall be determined through review by the relevant civic Circles following the completion of the residency period defined in Appendix III.
Citizenship represents the recognition that the resident has become a trusted and integrated member of the Society.
Section 7.07 — Granting of Citizenship
Citizenship shall be granted through a formal civic recognition process administered by the Circles responsible for governance and contribution.
Upon recognition as a citizen, the individual gains full civic rights and responsibilities within the Society, including participation in governance and constitutional decision‑making.
Citizenship affirms a mutual covenant between the individual and the community — a commitment to uphold the principles, responsibilities, and shared future of the Society.
Section 7.08 — Voluntary Withdrawal
Residents retain the right to voluntarily withdraw from the residency pathway at any time.
Individuals who determine that the Society’s civic framework does not align with their personal values or life goals may depart peacefully without penalty.
The Society recognizes that true consent requires the freedom to leave as well as the freedom to join.
Section 7.09 — Residency Termination
In rare circumstances, residency may be terminated if a resident demonstrates persistent incompatibility with the Society’s constitutional framework or engages in conduct that undermines civic harmony.
Such determinations must be reviewed by multiple civic Circles to ensure that termination decisions are not made arbitrarily or without due consideration.
Termination of residency shall be documented and communicated clearly to the resident, along with any available avenues for appeal or review.
The goal of the Residency Pathway is not exclusion but careful integration, ensuring that those who become citizens have demonstrated both commitment to the Society and respect for the principles that sustain it.
Article VIII — Citizenship Status
Citizenship within the Society represents the full recognition that an individual has become a trusted and integrated member of the community. It affirms that the individual has demonstrated sustained compatibility with the Society’s constitutional principles, civic expectations, cultural framework, and ecological responsibilities.
Citizenship is not granted as a symbolic designation alone. It reflects a mutual covenant between the individual and the Society, establishing both the rights of participation and the responsibilities necessary to sustain the community’s long‑term stability, harmony, and ecological balance.
This covenant recognizes that the health of the Society depends not only on laws and institutions, but on the character and participation of its citizens. Citizenship therefore represents a relationship of trust built through lived participation, contribution, and demonstrated respect for the Society’s civic principles.
Through citizenship, the individual becomes a permanent participant in the civic life of the Society and gains the authority to help guide its future through participation in governance, stewardship of shared resources, and collective decision‑making.
Citizenship also signifies that the individual has chosen to bind their future to that of the community. In return, the Society recognizes the citizen as a full and equal participant in its institutions, protections, and shared civic destiny.
Section 8.01 — Recognition of Citizenship
Citizenship shall be formally recognized following the successful completion of the Residency Pathway and the recommendation of the relevant civic Circles responsible for evaluating residency integration.
The recognition of citizenship shall occur through a formal civic acknowledgment process recorded within the Society’s governance archives. This recognition confirms that the individual has fulfilled the expectations of residency and has demonstrated the character, stability, and commitment necessary to join the community as a full citizen.
The acknowledgment of citizenship may include a civic recognition gathering or ceremonial acknowledgment reflecting the Society’s cultural traditions. Such recognition emphasizes that citizenship is not merely administrative, but represents the welcoming of a new permanent member into the community’s civic family.
Section 8.02 — Civic Rights
Citizens of the Society shall possess full civic rights as defined within the Constitution and associated charters of governance.
These rights include participation in civic assemblies, eligibility to vote within constitutional processes, and the ability to participate in the formation, operation, and oversight of civic Circles that guide the Society’s institutions.
Citizens may contribute to the development of policy, propose civic initiatives, participate in public deliberation, and engage in the stewardship of the Society’s shared institutions and resources.
Citizens also possess the right to transparency within governance, access to public civic records where appropriate, and the ability to participate meaningfully in discussions that influence the direction of the community.
These rights ensure that governance within the Society remains participatory, accountable, and rooted in the collective will of its citizens.
Section 8.03 — Civic Responsibilities
Citizenship carries responsibilities equal to its privileges. Citizens are expected to uphold the constitutional framework of the Society and to contribute to the maintenance of its civic systems.
Responsibilities include participation in systems of contribution appropriate to an individual’s abilities, respect for the principles of consent and restorative accountability, and stewardship of the ecological systems that sustain the community.
Citizens are also expected to participate constructively in civic dialogue, to resolve disagreements through restorative processes when conflicts arise, and to act in ways that strengthen civic trust and cooperation.
The stability of the Society depends on citizens who recognize that freedom and responsibility exist together. Through responsible participation, citizens ensure that the Society remains resilient, equitable, and sustainable for future generations.
Section 8.04 — Eligibility for Civic Roles
Citizens shall be eligible to serve within the Society’s civic institutions, including positions within the Circles responsible for governance, contribution, learning, health and healing, harmony, and other sectors established by constitutional charter.
Participation in these roles allows citizens to directly contribute to the administration, improvement, and ethical stewardship of the Society’s systems.
Eligibility for specific civic roles may require additional training, demonstrated experience, or selection procedures defined within the relevant civic institutions. These requirements exist to ensure that those entrusted with civic responsibilities possess the knowledge and judgment necessary to serve the community effectively.
Citizens serving within civic roles are expected to conduct themselves with integrity, transparency, and accountability to the community they represent.
Section 8.05 — Military and Civic Service
Citizens may be called to participate in forms of civic or defensive service as defined by the Society’s constitutional framework and defense structure.
Such service is intended to strengthen civic cohesion, preparedness, and collective responsibility rather than promote militarism. The Society maintains defensive capabilities solely to preserve its sovereignty, protect its people, and safeguard the stability of its institutions.
Participation in civic or defensive service also reinforces the principle that the preservation of the community is a shared responsibility. Through such service, citizens gain a deeper understanding of the responsibilities associated with safeguarding the Society and protecting the well‑being of its people.
Section 8.06 — Protection of Citizenship
Citizenship shall not be revoked arbitrarily. The loss of citizenship may only occur through processes defined within the Society’s justice framework and must involve review by the appropriate civic Circles.
These safeguards ensure that citizenship remains a stable and meaningful status while preserving the Society’s ability to address rare cases of severe civic incompatibility or violations of constitutional principles.
Any process that could result in the alteration or termination of citizenship must be conducted with transparency, procedural fairness, and careful review to protect the rights of the individual and the integrity of the Society’s governance system.
Section 8.07 — Voluntary Renunciation
Citizens retain the right to voluntarily renounce their citizenship should they choose to leave the Society permanently.
Renunciation shall be documented within the Society’s governance records to ensure clarity of legal and civic standing and to maintain accurate population and governance records.
Individuals who renounce citizenship may depart peacefully and without penalty, provided that no unresolved civic obligations remain outstanding.
The freedom to depart remains a fundamental element of the Society’s commitment to consent, autonomy, and the voluntary nature of civic belonging.
Section 8.08 — Continuity of Citizenship
Citizenship remains valid for the duration of an individual’s life unless voluntarily relinquished or altered through processes established within the Society’s constitutional justice framework.
This continuity reflects the Society’s recognition that citizenship represents a lasting relationship between the individual and the community, grounded in shared responsibility and mutual trust.
By establishing citizenship as a stable and enduring status, the Society reinforces the principle that membership in the community is not temporary or transactional, but a long‑term commitment between individuals and the society they help sustain.
Article IX — Loss of Citizenship and Independent Status
Citizenship within the Society represents a covenant of trust between the individual and the community. It reflects a relationship built upon participation, shared responsibility, and mutual respect for the constitutional principles that sustain the Society.
While citizenship is intended to be a stable and enduring status, circumstances may arise in which an individual can no longer remain a citizen within the Society’s civic framework. In such cases, the Society must balance compassion for the individual with responsibility to preserve the integrity, stability, and safety of the community as a whole.
The purpose of this article is to define the limited conditions under which citizenship may be relinquished, altered, or dissolved while preserving the Society’s commitment to fairness, due process, and human dignity.
Whenever possible, conflicts between citizens and the community shall first be addressed through restorative processes and mediation within the Society’s justice framework. These mechanisms are intended to repair harm, restore trust, and reintegrate individuals whenever reconciliation remains possible.
The loss of citizenship is therefore considered a final measure reserved for situations in which restoration, reconciliation, or continued compatibility is no longer achievable. Such outcomes are rare and treated with the utmost seriousness.
Section 9.01 — Voluntary Departure
Citizens retain the right to voluntarily leave the Society and relinquish their citizenship at any time. The freedom to depart is a foundational principle of a consent-based society and ensures that civic belonging remains voluntary rather than coercive.
Individuals choosing to depart shall notify the appropriate civic Circles so that their citizenship status may be formally recorded as renounced. This process ensures clarity of legal standing, maintains accurate civic records, and allows the Society to responsibly manage its population and governance structures.
Voluntary departure shall not be treated as punishment or failure. The Society recognizes that personal values, life goals, or life circumstances may evolve over time, and individuals must remain free to pursue paths that differ from those offered by the Society.
Citizens who depart peacefully may do so without stigma or hostility. The Society maintains that the right to leave is inseparable from the right to belong.
Section 9.02 — Civic Incompatibility
In rare circumstances, a citizen may demonstrate persistent incompatibility with the constitutional framework of the Society.
Such incompatibility may arise through repeated violation of core civic principles, refusal to participate in restorative processes, or sustained conduct that undermines the stability, trust, or well-being of the community.
Examples may include deliberate harm toward others, intentional disruption of civic institutions, or persistent refusal to recognize the principles of consent and restorative accountability that guide the Society’s justice framework.
Before any action affecting citizenship is considered, the Society shall make reasonable and documented efforts to pursue mediation, restorative accountability, and opportunities for reconciliation. These processes are intended to help individuals address conflict and reintegrate successfully within the community.
Only when such efforts have demonstrably failed may further review be considered.
Section 9.03 — Due Process Review
Any consideration of citizenship termination must undergo a formal review process involving multiple civic Circles.
This multi-circle review structure ensures that no single authority can unilaterally revoke citizenship or impose life-altering civic decisions without broader oversight.
Evidence, testimony, records of restorative proceedings, and documented patterns of conduct must be reviewed carefully before any determination is made.
The citizen involved shall be informed of the concerns raised and shall be given the opportunity to participate in the review process, present their perspective, and respond to the allegations under consideration.
This process protects both the individual and the Society by ensuring that decisions are made thoughtfully, transparently, and with appropriate accountability.
Section 9.04 — Determination of Status
Following review, the civic Circles may determine that one of the following outcomes is appropriate:
• restoration of full citizenship
• continuation of restorative oversight
• voluntary renunciation of citizenship
• transition to Independent status
The chosen outcome must reflect the best balance between restoration of the individual and preservation of the Society’s civic stability.
All determinations shall be documented within the Society’s governance archives to preserve transparency, historical accountability, and institutional memory.
Section 9.05 — Independent Status
An individual whose citizenship has been relinquished or dissolved may remain within the Society under the classification of Independent.
Independent individuals are recognized as residents who no longer participate in citizenship privileges or governance authority but who may continue living within the Society under defined conditions.
This status acknowledges that although an individual may no longer function within the civic covenant of citizenship, they remain a human being deserving of dignity and basic protections.
The designation of Independent status preserves human dignity while maintaining clarity regarding civic participation, responsibility, and the limits of governance authority.
Section 9.06 — Rights of Independents
Independents shall retain fundamental protections afforded to all persons within the Society.
These protections include access to basic shelter, healthcare, personal safety, and humane treatment under the Society’s justice framework.
However, Independents do not possess the civic authority associated with citizenship. They may not vote, participate in constitutional governance, or hold positions of authority within the Society’s civic Circles.
This distinction preserves the integrity of the Society’s governance system while ensuring that individuals are not subjected to deprivation, neglect, or abandonment.
The Society recognizes that dignity must extend even to those who no longer share its civic covenant.
Section 9.07 — Departure of Independents
Independents who determine that continued residence within the Society is not compatible with their personal goals or circumstances may depart peacefully.
Where feasible and appropriate, the Society may assist with logistical coordination to ensure safe and orderly departure from its territory.
Such assistance reflects the Society’s commitment to humane treatment and responsible stewardship of individuals who have lived within its community.
Section 9.08 — Finality of Citizenship Loss
The loss of citizenship represents a profound alteration of an individual’s relationship with the Society and shall therefore be treated with the utmost seriousness.
All decisions affecting citizenship status must be documented, reviewed, and preserved within the governance archives to ensure that the process remains transparent and accountable to the principles of justice upon which the Society is founded.
The Society recognizes that citizenship is built upon trust, participation, and shared commitment. The dissolution of that relationship is therefore undertaken only when all other paths toward restoration have been exhausted.
Through these safeguards, the Society affirms that even in moments of separation, justice must remain tempered by dignity, fairness, and respect for the individual.
Article X — Immigration Capacity Governance
The admission of new individuals into the Society shall be governed by the Society’s capacity to sustain population without degrading ecological balance, infrastructure stability, or civic well-being. Immigration policy must therefore operate within clearly defined capacity limits that protect both the well-being of existing citizens and the long-term sustainability of the Society’s institutions and natural systems.
Immigration capacity is determined through the Population Capacity Model established in Appendix I, the Operational Population Buffer Model established in Appendix II, and the Immigration Capacity Formula defined in Appendix III. These frameworks ensure that immigration policy remains aligned with ecological reality, infrastructure capacity, and responsible civic planning.
Population capacity shall always be constrained by the lowest limiting resource. Immigration decisions must therefore remain grounded in verifiable data rather than political pressure, ensuring that population growth never exceeds the Society’s ability to sustain it responsibly.
Section 10.01 — Purpose of Capacity Governance
Immigration within the Society shall be regulated through sustainable population limits. Admissions shall occur only when ecological capacity, infrastructure systems, and civic institutions can support additional population without degrading the stability or well-being of the community.
This governance structure ensures that immigration remains consistent with the Society’s long-term sustainability and prevents uncontrolled population growth that could strain resources or destabilize civic systems.
Section 10.02 — Capacity Determination
The Society shall determine its Maximum Sustainable Population (MSP) through the Population Capacity Model defined in Appendix I. This model evaluates the Society’s ecological carrying capacity and infrastructure limits across essential resource systems.
The model incorporates assessments of food production capability, water availability, housing infrastructure, healthcare capacity, energy production capability, educational infrastructure, and ecological sustainability.
The resulting MSP establishes the upper boundary of population that the Society can support without degrading environmental health or civic stability.
Section 10.03 — Operational Population Buffer
An Operational Population Buffer (OPB) shall be maintained to ensure that the Society does not operate at full population capacity. The buffer provides resilience against demographic fluctuations, ecological disruptions, and temporary infrastructure strain.
The methodology for determining and maintaining the buffer is defined in Appendix II.
Maintaining this buffer ensures that the Society retains the flexibility necessary to respond to unexpected events while preserving stable civic operations.
Section 10.04 — Available Immigration Capacity
The number of individuals who may be admitted into the Society during any civic cycle shall be determined through the Immigration Capacity Formula defined in Appendix III.
This calculation produces the Society’s Available Immigration Capacity (AIC), which represents the number of additional individuals who may be admitted without exceeding sustainable limits.
Admissions of Hopefuls and Transients shall not exceed the calculated AIC for that cycle.
Section 10.05 — Limiting Resource Principle
Population capacity shall always be determined by the lowest limiting resource. If any critical system approaches its sustainable limit, immigration capacity must be adjusted accordingly.
Limiting resources may include food production capability, water availability, housing infrastructure, healthcare capacity, energy production capability, educational infrastructure, and ecological carrying limits.
This principle ensures that population growth remains aligned with the Society’s ability to support its residents without degrading environmental or civic systems.
Section 10.06 — Capacity Assessment Authority
The Circles responsible for infrastructure and resource stewardship shall provide the data used in population capacity calculations which is calculated by the Circle of Balance. These include:
• Circle of Contribution
• Circle of Health and Healing
• Circle of Learning
These Circles shall conduct periodic assessments to ensure that population calculations remain accurate and reflect current conditions.
The variables used in the Immigration Capacity Formula shall be defined exclusively by the Population Capacity Model and Operational Population Buffer Model established in Appendices I and II.
These definitions may not be altered except through formal amendment to the Immigration Codex.
Section 10.07 — Recalculation Conditions
Population capacity may be recalculated prior to the next civic cycle if significant changes occur, including major infrastructure expansion, ecological disruption, demographic shifts, or changes in resource availability.
Recalculations must be supported by verifiable data provided by the relevant Circles responsible for the affected sectors.
Section 10.08 — Enforcement of Capacity Limits
Immigration admissions shall not exceed the calculated Available Immigration Capacity under any circumstance.
This safeguard ensures that immigration policy remains aligned with ecological sustainability, infrastructure stability, and the long-term well-being of the Society.
By maintaining strict adherence to capacity limits, the Society preserves the balance necessary for stable civic life while remaining open to new members who seek to participate in its shared covenant.
Article XI — Appeals and Review
